newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian poll victors appeal for rivals' support.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian poll victors appeal for rivals' support.

text.p: Bulgaria's jubilant election winners meet political rivals on Tuesday in the hope of winning their backing for harsh measures to rescue a bankrupt economy.

The reformist Union of Democratic Forces won an absolute majority in parliament in Saturday's polls and has no constitutional need for other parties' support, but wants a wide consensus for remedies that promise to be as painful as the disease.

"We are proposing that the newly-formed parliament pass an anti-crisis declaration, and tomorrow we start talks with the other main forces for agreement on its principles," UDF leader and prime minister-in-waiting Ivan Kostov told a news conference on Monday.

He said his priorities were carrying out reforms agreed with the International Monetary Fund, fighting organised crime and corruption, opening secret police files on public figures and bringing Bulgaria into the European Union and NATO.

Reforms include tight monetary discipline and privatisation. They look sure, at least in the short term, to increase unemployment, now at 14.5 percent, and further impoverish many Bulgarians already reeling from inflation of more than 2,000 percent a year.

The UDF won expressions of support from the small Euroleft group in parliament and hostile reaction from another, the Bulgarian Business Bloc. The response of a third small parliamentary group, the Union for National Salvation, was not yet clear.
But most crucial will be the response of the former ruling Socialists, a party of ex-communists who were forced from power by UDF-led unrest in January and February.
The Socialists, whose failure to launch reforms is blamed for the country's economic near-collapse, hold 57 seats in the new 240-seat parliament to the UDF's 137.

"I think dialogue with the Socialist Party is possible," Kostov said. "Anyway, I am optimistic that in the course of the talks we shall find the formula for agreement in the name of the country's future."

Kostov, however, raised a potentially explosive issue which could sour the mood in parliament by calling for communist-era secret police files on public figures to be opened, despite fears their contents are open to abuse.
"We are suggesting that files of members of parliament, cabinet ministers and supreme court judges should be opened, but only theirs," he said.
"We will proceed very cautiously with this matter, there won't be any humiliation, this will be only for high-profile politicians."

Critics of such a move point out that the seven years since the overthrow of communist dictatorship have been ample time for such files to be forged, amended or destroyed. Let sleeping dogs lie, they argue.

Electoral officials said the final official results of the Saturday poll might be announced on Tuesday. Foreign election monitors from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe on Monday declared the poll free and fair.

The first task of the new parliament will be to pass a 1997 budget and package of banking laws needed to implement a currency board, a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime agreed with the IMF as a condition for a $657 million funding deal.

Bulgarian Brady bonds rose sharply on the secondary debt market on the news of the UDF victory. The battered lev currency traded lower on the interbank market, but Finance Minister Svetoslav Gavriiski blamed speculation, saying traders were buying dollars in anticipation of a lev fall.
